labs.title: Disk full, but du finds only half of it
labs.symptom: A service reports `No space left on device` when it writes to `/mnt/labdisk`. You have a shell on the server. Find what is using the space and free it **without losing data**.
build: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/labdisk
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=16m tmpfs /mnt/labdisk
sudo chown $(id -un): /mnt/labdisk
mkdir /mnt/labdisk/app /mnt/labdisk/backup
dd if=/dev/zero of=/mnt/labdisk/backup/old-dump.sql bs=1M count=6 status=none
dd if=/dev/zero of=/mnt/labdisk/app/app.log bs=1M count=9 status=none
(sleep 600 < /mnt/labdisk/app/app.log > /dev/null 2>&1 &)
rm /mnt/labdisk/app/app.log
dd if=/dev/zero of=/mnt/labdisk/app/cache.bin bs=1M count=100 status=none 2>/dev/null || true
teardown: lsof -t +aL1 /mnt/labdisk 2>/dev/null | xargs -r kill ; sudo umount -l /mnt/labdisk ; sudo rmdir /mnt/labdisk ; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** Writes fail with `No space left on device`. What do you run first?

choices.note: Good first move. It confirms the filesystem is 100% full and shows its size.
choices.output:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
tmpfs            16M   16M     0 100% /mnt/labdisk

choices.note: Shows the top-level directories, but not how much space is used or free. Check `df` first.
choices.output:
total 0
drwxrwxrwt. 4 opc  opc  80 Nov  8 19:28 .
drwxr-xr-x. 3 root root 21 Nov  8 19:28 ..
drwxr-xr-x. 2 opc  opc  60 Nov  8 19:28 app
drwxr-xr-x. 2 opc  opc  60 Nov  8 19:28 backup

choices.note: A reboot interrupts every service and may not even help: files on disk stay. Never reboot before you know the cause.
choices.reason: destructive on a real server, so it was not run

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** `df` says the filesystem is full. What is using the space?

choices.note: Right tool. But compare the sizes with the `Used` column of `df`. They do not match.
Checks inodes. This is the right idea when a disk is "full" but `df -h` shows free space. Here the blocks themselves are full, so this is not the cause.
choices.output:
Filesystem     Inodes IUsed  IFree IUse% Mounted on
tmpfs          722241     7 722234    1% /mnt/labdisk

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** `du` adds up to less than `df` reports. Which command finds the missing space?

choices.note: Finds files that still have a name. The missing space has no name any more, so `find` cannot see it.

`+L1` lists open files with link count below 1: deleted files that a process still holds open. `+a` limits the list to this filesystem. The `NLINK 0` column and `(deleted)` mark the file. Its space is not freed until the process closes it.
choices.output:
COMMAND    PID USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME
sleep   424485  opc    0r   REG  0,132  9437184     0    5 /mnt/labdisk/app/app.log (deleted)

choices.note: Deleting the backup destroys data and does not fix the cause. Free space only after you know what holds it.
choices.reason: it would delete a backup, so it was not run

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** A deleted `app.log` (9 MB) is still open in a process. In real life you restart the service that holds it. Here the holder is a `sleep` process, and `lsof -t` prints just its PID. What do you do?

choices.note: Ending the holder closes the file. The kernel then frees the blocks. On a real server, restart or reload the service so it reopens its log.

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Verify the space is back.

choices.note: Space was freed with no data lost.
choices.output:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
tmpfs            16M  7.0M  9.0M  44% /mnt/labdisk

labs.conclusion: The log file was deleted, but a running process still had it open. A file's data is freed only when its **last name is removed and the last open file descriptor is closed**. `du` walks names, so it missed the file. `df` asks the filesystem, so it counted the blocks. `lsof +L1` finds exactly this case. See [deleted but open](#/lesson/18/deleted-but-open).

labs.title: High load average, but the CPU is idle
labs.symptom: Monitoring shows the load average climbing and users say the application hangs, but the CPU graph is flat and low. The application reads files from an NFS mount, `/mnt/labnfs`. You have a shell.
build: sudo mkdir -p /srv/lab-nfs && echo data | sudo tee /srv/lab-nfs/f > /dev/null && sudo chown $(id -un): /srv/lab-nfs
echo '/srv/lab-nfs 127.0.0.1(rw,sync,no_subtree_check)' | sudo tee /etc/exports.d/lab.exports > /dev/null; sudo systemctl start nfs-server
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/labnfs && sudo mount -t nfs4 -o hard,timeo=5 127.0.0.1:/srv/lab-nfs /mnt/labnfs
for i in 1 2 3 4; do (while true; do cat /mnt/labnfs/f > /dev/null; sleep 0.2; done) & done; sleep 1
sudo systemctl stop nfs-server; sleep 25
teardown: sudo systemctl start nfs-server; sleep 2; kill $(jobs -p) 2>/dev/null; sleep 1; sudo umount /mnt/labnfs || sudo umount -l /mnt/labnfs; sudo exportfs -ua; sudo rm -f /etc/exports.d/lab.exports; sudo systemctl stop nfs-server; sudo rm -rf /srv/lab-nfs; sudo rmdir /mnt/labnfs; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** What do you run first?

choices.note: Confirms the load is well above normal (it was about 0.3). Load counts runnable **and** uninterruptible tasks.
Rebooting hides the cause and the hang returns when the NFS server is down again.
choices.reason: destructive on a real server, so it was not run

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** Load is high. Is the CPU busy?

choices.note: Shows the CPU time breakdown: almost everything is idle. So the load is not from running tasks.
Idle CPU confirmed. Note that the `b` column may show 0 here: tasks stuck in a killable wait are in `D` state but are not always counted there. That is why `ps` is more reliable.

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** Idle CPU and high load: tasks must be in D state (uninterruptible sleep). List them with the kernel function they wait in.

choices.note: Four `cat` processes in `D` state, waiting in `rpc_wait_bit_killable`: an RPC call (NFS) that does not complete.
The busiest tasks use only a few percent: nothing is consuming the CPU. The stuck tasks use no CPU at all. Look at process **state** instead.

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** The waiting function is an RPC wait. Which mounts could be involved? (Be careful: some commands hang on a dead mount.)

choices.note: Reads the mount table without touching the mount, so it cannot hang. There is an NFS mount, mounted **hard**: the client retries forever.
`df` calls `statfs` on the dead mount and would itself hang in D state. Never run it on a suspect NFS mount.
choices.reason: it would hang this shell in D state

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** The NFS server is down. Bring it back.

choices.note: Starting the server lets the pending RPCs complete. The blocked tasks resume. Doing this beats killing the clients, which would only restart the problem.
SIGKILL can end tasks in a killable wait, but the application starts new readers that hang again. It treats the symptom.
choices.reason: it does not remove the cause, and the readers are restarted by the application

steps.prompt: **Step 6.** Verify.

choices.note: No task is in D state any more. The load average will decay over the next minutes.

labs.conclusion: A **hard NFS mount** makes tasks wait forever when the server is unreachable. They sit in uninterruptible sleep (`D`), which counts toward the load average without using CPU. The tells: high load, idle CPU, `D` tasks in `rpc_*` wait functions, and an NFS mount. Fix the server or network, not the clients. See [process states](#/lesson/10/process-states) and [NFS](#/lesson/23/nfs-loopback).

labs.title: A service keeps restarting: OOM kills
labs.symptom: The service `lab-leak` restarts every few seconds. Nobody changed the deployment. The server has plenty of free memory.
build:
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/lab-leak.py > /dev/null <<'EOF'
import time
data = []
while True:
    data.append(b'x' * (5 << 20))
    time.sleep(0.2)
EOF

printf '[Unit]
Description=Lab leaking service

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/lab-leak.py
MemoryMax=60M
MemorySwapMax=0
Restart=always
RestartSec=1
' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/lab-leak.service > /dev/null; sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start lab-leak; sleep 12
teardown: sudo systemctl stop lab-leak; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-leak.service /usr/local/bin/lab-leak.py; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** What is the service doing?

choices.note: It is flapping between `activating (auto-restart)` and `active`, and the previous run ended with `code=killed, status=9/KILL`: something sent SIGKILL.
choices.output:
Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/lab-leak.service; static)
    Drop-In: /run/systemd/system.control/lab-leak.service.d
             └─50-MemoryMax.conf
     Active: activating (auto-restart) (Result: oom-kill) since Sun 2026-11-08 19:29:13 GMT; 227ms ago
    Process: 427097 ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/lab-leak.py (code=killed, signal=KILL)

choices.note: Restarting hides the evidence and changes nothing: it will die again.
choices.reason: it would only restart the failure loop

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** SIGKILL, but who sent it? What does the unit's log say?

choices.cmd: journalctl -u lab-leak -o cat --no-pager | grep -E 'killed|OOM|Failed with|exited' | tail -n 3
choices.note: systemd says the process was killed by the **OOM killer**.
choices.output:
lab-leak.service: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer.
lab-leak.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
lab-leak.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.

choices.note: The service itself prints nothing: it is killed without a message.
choices.output:
lab-leak.service: A process of this unit has been killed by the OOM killer.
lab-leak.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
lab-leak.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** The host has free memory, yet the OOM killer acted. Check the kernel log.

choices.cmd: sudo dmesg | grep -i 'memory cgroup out of memory' | tail -n 1 | sed -E 's/^\[[^]]*\] //' | cut -c1-120
choices.note: `Memory cgroup out of memory`: not the machine, the service's **cgroup** hit its limit.
choices.output: Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 427097 (python3) total-vm:534472kB, anon-rss:306452kB, file-rss:16636kB, shm

choices.note: The machine has plenty of memory. This is why the problem is confusing: the limit is per service.
choices.output:
total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            5642        3614         354          25        1875        2028

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** Which limit applies and how often has it been reached?

choices.note: `memory.max` is 62914560 (60 MB) and `NRestarts` shows how often systemd has restarted the service. (The cgroup's own `memory.events` counters start from zero after each restart, so they would show 0 here.)

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Decide. The service is leaking memory (RSS grows steadily until the limit). What do you do right now?

choices.note: Stop the flapping service so it does not disturb the rest, and give the developers the evidence. The leak itself must be fixed in the code.
A band-aid: it buys time, but the leak continues and will hit the new limit later. Acceptable only with a ticket to fix the leak.

labs.conclusion: Exit status 137 / `status=9/KILL` plus `Memory cgroup out of memory` in the kernel log means the **service's own memory limit** was reached, not a shortage on the host. Read `memory.events` and `memory.max` of the unit's cgroup, watch RSS over time to see a leak, and fix the application. Raising the limit only postpones the problem. See [memory and OOM](#/lesson/15/mmap-and-oom) and [cgroups](#/lesson/38/cgroup-v2-hands-on).

labs.title: "Too many open files"
labs.symptom: After a deployment the service `lab-fd` logs an error at startup and does not serve requests. It worked on the old server.
build:
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/lab-fd.py > /dev/null <<'EOF'
import time
files = []
try:
    for _ in range(100):
        files.append(open('/dev/null'))
    print('ready: holding %d files' % len(files), flush=True)
except OSError as e:
    print('ERROR: %s after %d files' % (e, len(files)), flush=True)
time.sleep(3600)
EOF

printf '[Unit]
Description=Lab fd service

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /usr/local/bin/lab-fd.py
LimitNOFILE=40
DynamicUser=yes
' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/lab-fd.service > /dev/null; sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start lab-fd; sleep 2
teardown: sudo systemctl stop lab-fd; sudo rm -rf /etc/systemd/system/lab-fd.service /etc/systemd/system/lab-fd.service.d /usr/local/bin/lab-fd.py; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** What does the service say?

choices.note: `Too many open files` after 37 files: the process hit the descriptor limit (EMFILE).
choices.output:
/etc/systemd/system/lab-fd.service:7: Special user nobody configured, this is not safe!
Started Lab fd service.
ERROR: [Errno 24] Too many open files: '/dev/null' after 37 files

choices.note: It is `active`: the process still runs, but it is useless. A running process does not mean a working service.

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** Which limit applies to **the service**? (Your shell's limit is not the service's.)

choices.note: That is the limit of **your shell**, probably very high. Services get their limits from the unit, not from your login.

choices.cmd: grep 'Max open files' /proc/$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value lab-fd)/limits
choices.note: The running process has a soft and hard limit of **40**.

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** Where does the 40 come from, and how many descriptors are in use?

choices.cmd: systemctl show lab-fd -p LimitNOFILE; sudo ls /proc/$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value lab-fd)/fd | wc -l
choices.note: `LimitNOFILE=40` is set in the unit file, and the process holds about 40 descriptors (the limit; `sudo` is needed because the service runs as another user). This is a configuration problem, not a leak.

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** The application legitimately needs about 100 descriptors. Fix the limit with a drop-in, not by editing the vendor file.

choices.cmd: sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/lab-fd.service.d && printf '[Service]\nLimitNOFILE=1024\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/lab-fd.service.d/override.conf > /dev/null && sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart lab-fd; sleep 2; journalctl -u lab-fd -o cat --no-pager | tail -n 1
choices.note: A drop-in survives package updates. After a restart the service is ready with its 100 files.
`ulimit` changes your shell only. The service is started by systemd and ignores it.
choices.reason: it would not change the service's limit

labs.conclusion: `Too many open files` is `EMFILE`: the process reached its soft `RLIMIT_NOFILE`. For services the limit comes from `LimitNOFILE=` in the unit (not from your shell), and `/proc/PID/limits` shows what the **running** process has. Raise it with a drop-in, restart, and check. If the descriptor count keeps growing without load, look for a leak instead. See [file descriptors](#/lesson/17/too-many-open-files).

labs.title: The service won't start
labs.symptom: `systemctl start lab-web` fails. The package was just installed and nothing else changed.
build:
sudo tee /usr/local/bin/lab-web-server.sh > /dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "lab-web serving on port 8080"
exec sleep 3600
EOF
sudo chmod 644 /usr/local/bin/lab-web-server.sh

printf '[Unit]
Description=Lab web service

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/lab-webd
' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/lab-web.service > /dev/null; sudo systemctl daemon-reload
teardown: sudo systemctl stop lab-web 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-web.service /usr/local/bin/lab-web-server.sh; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** Start it and look at the result.

choices.cmd: sudo systemctl start lab-web 2>&1 | sed 's/ See .*//'; systemctl is-failed lab-web
choices.note: The job failed. systemd tells you where to look next.

choices.cmd: sudo systemctl restart lab-web && echo started
choices.note: Repeating the command gives no new information, and note the trap: it even printed `started`. For a `Type=simple` service systemctl reports success once the process is forked; the 203/EXEC failure appears a moment later. Always read the status and the journal.

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** What is the failure?

choices.note: `status=203/EXEC`: systemd could not **execute** the program. 203 is the exec failure of systemd itself, before the service even runs.
choices.output:
Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Sun 2026-11-08 19:29:32 GMT; 422ms ago
    Process: 428630 ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/lab-webd (code=exited, status=203/EXEC)

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** Why could it not be executed?

choices.cmd: journalctl -u lab-web -o cat --no-pager | grep -E 'Failed to (locate|execute)' | tail -n 1 | cut -c1-120
choices.note: `Failed to locate executable /usr/local/bin/lab-webd: No such file or directory`. The path in the unit is wrong.
choices.output: lab-web.service: Failed to locate executable /usr/local/bin/lab-webd: No such file or directory

choices.note: Disabling SELinux is a reaction, not a diagnosis. The log already says the file does not exist.
choices.reason: it weakens the system and is unrelated here

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** What files exist, and what does the unit say?

choices.cmd: ls /usr/local/bin/ | grep lab-web; systemctl cat lab-web --no-pager | grep ExecStart
choices.note: The script is called `lab-web-server.sh`, but `ExecStart` points to `lab-webd`. A typo in the path.

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Fix the path in the unit and try again.

choices.cmd: sudo sed -i 's#/usr/local/bin/lab-webd#/usr/local/bin/lab-web-server.sh#' /etc/systemd/system/lab-web.service; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; sudo systemctl start lab-web 2>&1 | sed 's/ See .*//'; sleep 1; journalctl -u lab-web -o cat --no-pager | grep -E 'Failed to (locate|execute)' | tail -n 1 | cut -c1-120
choices.note: A different error now: **Permission denied**. systemd found the file but it is not executable. Two causes were hiding behind one symptom.
choices.output: lab-web.service: Failed to locate executable /usr/local/bin/lab-webd: No such file or directory

steps.prompt: **Step 6.** Check the file mode, fix it and start the service.

choices.cmd: ls -l /usr/local/bin/lab-web-server.sh | cut -c1-10; sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/lab-web-server.sh; sudo systemctl start lab-web; sleep 1; systemctl is-active lab-web
choices.note: Mode was 644 (no execute bit). With 755 the service is `active`.

labs.conclusion: Read the **exit status** first: `203/EXEC` means systemd could not run the `ExecStart` program (missing file, bad path, no execute permission, wrong interpreter, SELinux). The journal line names the exact reason. Fix one cause at a time and test again: a second error is progress. Use `systemctl cat` to see the real unit and `systemd-analyze verify` before starting. See [writing a service](#/lesson/25/write-a-service).

labs.title: Everything takes five seconds: slow DNS
labs.symptom: Every first connection from the client host takes ten seconds. Connecting by IP address is instant. The client host is the namespace `lab-dns`.
build: for n in lab-dns lab-ns; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; sudo rm -rf /etc/netns/lab-dns; true
sudo ip netns add lab-dns; sudo ip netns add lab-ns; sudo ip link add vd type veth peer name vn; sudo ip link set vd netns lab-dns; sudo ip link set vn netns lab-ns

sudo ip -n lab-dns addr add 10.200.6.1/24 dev vd; sudo ip -n lab-ns addr add 10.200.6.2/24 dev vn; sudo ip -n lab-ns addr add 10.200.6.9/24 dev vn; for n in lab-dns lab-ns; do sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done; sudo ip -n lab-dns link set vd up; sudo ip -n lab-ns link set vn up

sudo ip netns exec lab-ns nft add table ip f; sudo ip netns exec lab-ns nft 'add chain ip f in { type filter hook input priority 0; }'; sudo ip netns exec lab-ns nft add rule ip f in ip daddr 10.200.6.9 drop
sudo mkdir -p /etc/netns/lab-dns; printf 'nameserver 10.200.6.9\nnameserver 10.200.6.2\n' | sudo tee /etc/netns/lab-dns/resolv.conf > /dev/null

cat > /tmp/lab/dns53.py <<'EOF'
import socket, struct
ANSWERS = {'lab.example.': '10.200.8.8'}


def name(data, pos):
    labels = []
    while data[pos]:
        n = data[pos]
        labels.append(data[pos + 1:pos + 1 + n].decode())
        pos += n + 1
    return '.'.join(labels) + '.', pos + 1


s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(('10.200.6.2', 53))
while True:
    data, who = s.recvfrom(512)
    q, end = name(data, 12)
    qtype = struct.unpack('!H', data[end:end + 2])[0]
    ip = ANSWERS.get(q.lower())
    reply = data[:2] + struct.pack('!HHHHH', 0x8180 if ip else 0x8183, 1, 1 if ip and qtype == 1 else 0, 0, 0) + data[12:end + 4]
    if ip and qtype == 1:
        reply += b'\xc0\x0c' + struct.pack('!HHIH', 1, 1, 60, 4) + socket.inet_aton(ip)
    s.sendto(reply, who)
EOF
sudo ip netns exec lab-ns python3 /tmp/lab/dns53.py > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo $! > /tmp/lab/dns53.pid; sleep 1; true
teardown: sudo kill $(cat /tmp/lab/dns53.pid) 2>/dev/null; for n in lab-dns lab-ns; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; sudo rm -rf /etc/netns/lab-dns; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** Measure the delay the way programs experience it.

choices.cmd: { TIMEFORMAT='%R s'; time sudo ip netns exec lab-dns getent hosts lab.example; } 2>&1
choices.note: The lookup succeeds but takes about **10 seconds**: timeouts somewhere in the resolver path (the default timeout is 5 seconds, and here two of them were needed).

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-dns ping -c 1 -W 1 10.200.8.8
choices.note: There is no route to that address from the client in this lab. The question is about **name** resolution, not connectivity.

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** Which DNS servers does the client use, and in which order?

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-dns cat /etc/resolv.conf
choices.note: Two nameservers. The resolver asks the **first** one and waits for its timeout (5 s by default) before trying the second.

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** Ask each server directly, with a short timeout.

choices.cmd: dig @10.200.6.9 lab.example +time=1 +tries=1 +short 2>&1 | head -n 1; echo "(first server) exit: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
choices.note: dig run from the host cannot reach the lab network, so this proves nothing: query from **inside** the client namespace.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-dns dig @10.200.6.9 lab.example +time=1 +tries=1 +short 2>&1 | head -n 1
choices.note: The first server does not answer at all (a timeout, not an error): it is **dead or filtered**.

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** And the second server?

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-dns dig @10.200.6.2 lab.example +short
choices.note: The second server answers immediately. The delay is the dead first server.

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Fix the resolver configuration.

choices.cmd:
printf 'nameserver 10.200.6.2
nameserver 10.200.6.9
options timeout:1 attempts:1
' | sudo tee /etc/netns/lab-dns/resolv.conf > /dev/null; { TIMEFORMAT='%R s'; time sudo ip netns exec lab-dns getent hosts lab.example; } 2>&1
choices.note: Working server first, dead one last, and a short timeout: the lookup is instant. Better still: remove the dead server or repair it.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-dns systemctl restart NetworkManager
choices.note: Restarting services does not change a dead nameserver entry.
choices.reason: no such service exists in the namespace and it would not help

labs.conclusion: The resolver (`getaddrinfo`) tries the nameservers **in order**, waiting `timeout` (default 5 s) for each. A dead first nameserver adds at least one timeout (5 s by default, and the resolver may need several) to **every** lookup. Diagnose with `time getent hosts NAME` (what programs see), then `dig @each-server NAME` to find the silent one. Fix by removing or repairing it, reordering, and lowering `timeout`/`attempts`. See [name resolution](#/lesson/30/name-resolution).

labs.title: The service times out, but ping works
labs.symptom: From the client `lab-a`, `curl http://10.200.2.2:8080/` times out. The server runs on `lab-c`, behind a router `lab-b`. Colleagues say the network team changed something on the router.
build: for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; true
for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done

sudo ip link add va type veth peer name vb1; sudo ip link set va netns lab-a; sudo ip link set vb1 netns lab-b; sudo ip link add vb2 type veth peer name vc; sudo ip link set vb2 netns lab-b; sudo ip link set vc netns lab-c

sudo ip -n lab-a addr add 10.200.1.1/24 dev va; sudo ip -n lab-b addr add 10.200.1.2/24 dev vb1; sudo ip -n lab-b addr add 10.200.2.1/24 dev vb2; sudo ip -n lab-c addr add 10.200.2.2/24 dev vc; for d in 'lab-a va' 'lab-b vb1' 'lab-b vb2' 'lab-c vc'; do set -- $d; sudo ip -n $1 link set $2 up; done
sudo ip netns exec lab-b sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1; sudo ip -n lab-a route add 10.200.2.0/24 via 10.200.1.2; sudo ip -n lab-c route add 10.200.1.0/24 via 10.200.2.1
sudo ip netns exec lab-c python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.200.2.2 > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo $! > /tmp/lab/srv.pid; sleep 1; true

sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft add table ip filter; sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft 'add chain ip filter forward { type filter hook forward priority 0; policy accept; }'; sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft add rule ip filter forward tcp dport 8080 counter drop
teardown: sudo kill $(cat /tmp/lab/srv.pid) 2>/dev/null; for n in lab-a lab-b lab-c; do sudo ip netns del $n 2>/dev/null; done; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** Reproduce the problem and note the exact symptom.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-a curl -s -m 3 -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.2.2:8080/; echo "curl exit code: $?"
choices.note: Exit code 28: a **timeout**. Not `refused` (7) and not `unreachable`: packets vanish silently.

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** Is the network path itself working?

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-a ping -c 2 -W 1 10.200.2.2 | grep transmitted | sed -E 's/, time [0-9]+ms//'
choices.note: Ping works: routing, forwarding and the server host are fine. Only **this TCP port** is affected.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-a traceroute -n -q1 -w1 -m 3 10.200.2.2 | awk 'NR>1 {print $1, $2}'
choices.note: The path is two hops and both answer (ICMP). Consistent with a problem that is specific to the port.

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** Try the port from the client with a short timeout, then from the server's own side.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-a nc -zv -w 2 10.200.2.2 8080 2>&1 | grep -v Version | sed -E 's/^Ncat: //'
choices.note: Times out too: same symptom as curl.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-c curl -s -m 3 -o /dev/null -w 'on the server itself: http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.2.2:8080/
choices.note: The service works **locally**. So the application is fine and packets are lost between client and server.

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** Where are they lost? Capture on both sides of the router while the client tries.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b timeout 4 tcpdump -i vb1 -nn -l 'tcp port 8080' -c 1 2>/dev/null | sed -E 's/^[0-9:.]+ IP //; s/, seq.*//' > in.txt & A=$!; sudo ip netns exec lab-b timeout 4 tcpdump -i vb2 -nn -l 'tcp port 8080' 2>/dev/null | wc -l > out.txt & B=$!; sleep 1; sudo ip netns exec lab-a curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null http://10.200.2.2:8080/; wait $A $B; echo "in:  $(sed -E 's/[0-9]{5}/PORT/' in.txt)"; echo "out: $(cat out.txt) packets"
choices.note: The SYN **arrives** on the client side of the router but **nothing leaves** on the server side. The router itself discards it.

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** What is on the router?

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft list ruleset | sed -E 's/packets [0-9]+ bytes [0-9]+/packets N bytes N/'
choices.note: A `forward` rule drops `tcp dport 8080`, and its counter shows it matching. Ping is not TCP, so it passed.

steps.prompt: **Step 6.** Remove the rule (after agreeing with the network team) and verify.

choices.cmd: sudo ip netns exec lab-b nft flush ruleset; sudo ip netns exec lab-a curl -s -m 3 -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}\n' http://10.200.2.2:8080/
choices.note: The service answers again.

labs.conclusion: `Connection timed out` with a working ping means the path is fine and **something drops that port**. Prove the service works locally, then capture **both sides of each device on the path**: a packet that enters but never leaves was dropped there. `nft list ruleset` counters confirm which rule matched. See [network troubleshooting](#/lesson/32/tcpdump-mtr-curl).

labs.title: Zombie processes keep piling up
labs.symptom: A monitoring alert says the number of `<defunct>` processes on the server is growing. Nothing has crashed yet, but the PID table is slowly filling.
build: gcc -o /tmp/lab/zmaker /tmp/lab/zmaker.c
nohup /tmp/lab/zmaker > /dev/null 2>&1 & echo $! > /tmp/lab/zm.pid; sleep 5; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** How many zombies are there?

choices.note: A growing number of processes in state `Z`.
Works, but counting by state is cleaner and does not match the grep itself.

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** Zombies are already dead. Who is responsible for them?

choices.cmd: ps -eo ppid,stat | awk '$2 ~ /^Z/ {c[$1]++} END {for (p in c) print "parent", p, "has", c[p], "zombies"}' | sed -E 's/parent [0-9]+/parent PID/'
choices.note: All zombies belong to **one parent**. Its children exit and it never calls `wait`.
You cannot kill a zombie: it is already dead. The signal has nobody to run in. The entry stays until the parent calls `wait`.

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** Identify the parent process.

choices.note: The parent is `zmaker` and it is running normally (state `S`): a program that forks and never reaps its children.

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** What fixes the zombies?

choices.note: With the parent gone, the zombies are re-parented to PID 1, which reaps them at once: count 0. The real fix is in the application (handle `SIGCHLD` and call `wait`), then restart it.
A reboot also clears them, but needlessly interrupts everything and the bug returns.
choices.reason: destructive on a real server, so it was not run

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Verify nothing remains.

choices.note: No zombies.

labs.conclusion: A zombie is a finished child whose parent has not collected its exit status. It uses no CPU or memory except a PID slot, and **cannot be killed**. Count them by parent (`ps -eo ppid,stat`), then fix or restart the **parent**; PID 1 reaps the orphaned zombies. Long-term: the application must `wait()`, and containers need an init that reaps. See [zombies](#/lesson/10/zombies-orphans).

labs.title: A filesystem turned read-only
labs.symptom: An application on `/mnt/labro` suddenly fails with `Read-only file system`, though nobody remounted anything. The disk is a device-mapper volume.
build: truncate -s 64M /tmp/lab/ro.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show /tmp/lab/ro.img); echo $L > /tmp/lab/ro.loop; S=$(sudo blockdev --getsz $L); echo "0 $S linear $L 0" | sudo dmsetup create labro

sudo mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/mapper/labro; sudo tune2fs -e remount-ro /dev/mapper/labro > /dev/null; sudo mkdir -p /mnt/labro && sudo mount /dev/mapper/labro /mnt/labro && sudo chown $(id -un): /mnt/labro; echo ok > /mnt/labro/a.txt; sync

L=$(cat /tmp/lab/ro.loop); S=$(sudo blockdev --getsz $L); sudo dmsetup suspend --noflush labro && echo "0 $S error" | sudo dmsetup load labro && sudo dmsetup resume labro; echo more > /mnt/labro/b.txt; sync; sleep 1; true
teardown: sudo umount -l /mnt/labro 2>/dev/null; sudo dmsetup remove --force labro 2>/dev/null; sudo losetup -d $(cat /tmp/lab/ro.loop) 2>/dev/null; sudo rmdir /mnt/labro 2>/dev/null; true

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** Confirm the symptom.

choices.note: `Read-only file system`: writes are refused.
choices.output: touch: cannot touch '/mnt/labro/new.txt': Read-only file system

choices.note: Permissions are not the problem (the error is `Read-only file system`, not `Permission denied`) and chmod would fail the same way.
choices.reason: it would fail with the same error and does not address the cause

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** Why did it become read-only? Ask the kernel.

choices.cmd: sudo dmesg | grep -E 'EXT4-fs.*(error|Remounting|I/O error)' | tail -n 3 | sed -E 's/^\[[^]]*\] //; s/dm-[0-9]+/dm-N/' | cut -c1-110
choices.note: `Detected aborted journal`, `I/O error while writing superblock`, `Remounting filesystem read-only`. ext4 was configured with `errors=remount-ro`: after an I/O error it protects the data by going read-only.
choices.output:
EXT4-fs error (device dm-N): ext4_journal_check_start:86: comm ext4lazyinit: Detected aborted journal
EXT4-fs (dm-N): I/O error while writing superblock
EXT4-fs (dm-N): Remounting filesystem read-only

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** An I/O error comes from below the file system. Look at the device.

choices.cmd: sudo dmsetup status labro | sed -E 's/[0-9]+ ([0-9]+) /0 \1 /' | awk '{print $3}'
choices.note: The device-mapper target is `error`: every I/O to the device fails. In real life this could be a dead path (multipath), a failing disk, a detached cloud volume or a SAN fault.
Never run fsck on a **mounted** file system. And the file system is not the root cause: the device below is failing.
choices.reason: running fsck on a mounted file system can corrupt it

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** Repair in the right order: stop using the file system, restore the device, check, remount.

choices.note: Unmounted. Now it is safe to touch the device.

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Restore the device (here: switch the table back to the real mapping) and check the file system.

choices.cmd: L=$(cat /tmp/lab/ro.loop); S=$(sudo blockdev --getsz $L); echo "0 $S linear $L 0" | sudo dmsetup load labro && sudo dmsetup resume labro; sudo dmsetup status labro | awk '{print $3}'; sudo e2fsck -fy /dev/mapper/labro 2>&1 | tail -n 1 | sed -E 's#/dev/[a-z0-9/-]+#DEV#'
choices.note: The device works again, and `e2fsck` finishes (the journal is replayed or the file system is clean).

steps.prompt: **Step 6.** Mount it again and test.

choices.cmd: sudo mount /dev/mapper/labro /mnt/labro && sudo chown $(id -un): /mnt/labro && touch /mnt/labro/new.txt && echo 'write works again'
choices.note: Writable again.

labs.conclusion: A file system that went read-only did so **on purpose**, after an I/O or metadata error (`errors=remount-ro`). Read `dmesg` for the first error, find the failing layer **below** it (disk, RAID, multipath, cloud volume), repair that, then `umount`, `fsck`, `mount`. Remounting read-write without understanding the error risks corrupting data. See [filesystems](#/lesson/20/journal-fsck-cow).

labs.title: A server that won't boot (explanation only)
labs.symptom: After a reboot following a kernel update, the server stops at `Dropping to initramfs shell`. The console shows `dracut-initqueue: timeout, still waiting for /dev/mapper/vg-root`. This lab is **explanation only**: it needs a machine that does not boot, which cannot be created safely here, so no output is recorded.

steps.prompt: **Step 1.** Which stage failed, and what is the first thing to check in the recovery shell?

choices.note: The kernel started and the initramfs is running, so firmware, boot loader and kernel worked. Check the command line: is `root=` and `rd.lvm.lv=` what you expect?
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

choices.note: Rebooting repeats the failure and may lose the console messages.
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

steps.prompt: **Step 2.** The root logical volume is not found. Are the disks and the volume group visible?

choices.note: If the disk is missing, the initramfs lacks a driver (new kernel without the storage module) or the device is gone. If the disk is there but the VG is inactive, activate it.
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

steps.prompt: **Step 3.** The disk is visible and the VG is inactive. Activate it and continue.

choices.note: With the root LV active the boot continues. But it will fail again next time: you must fix the cause (usually the initramfs).
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

choices.note: Creating a file system destroys the data. Never format to "fix" a boot problem.
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

steps.prompt: **Step 4.** After booting, make it permanent. The initramfs of the new kernel was built without the needed driver.

choices.note: Rebuild the initramfs for the running kernel and verify the storage modules are inside.
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

steps.prompt: **Step 5.** Make the next boot safe.

choices.note: Know which kernels are installed, keep the previous one as a fallback, and test the new one once with `grub2-reboot`.
choices.reason: needs a machine that does not boot; shown as the command you would run in the recovery shell

labs.conclusion: Where the boot stops tells you the stage: before GRUB (firmware, ESP), at GRUB (menu, config), kernel panic (kernel, root device), **`Dropping to initramfs`** (the initramfs could not find or mount the root: missing driver, wrong `root=`/`rd.*`, inactive LVM/RAID, bad fstab). Fix from the dracut shell or a rescue boot, then rebuild the initramfs and keep a known-good kernel. See [the boot process](#/lesson/24/boot-sequence) and [boot debugging](#/lesson/24/boot-debugging).
